question: What viscosity range must fuel oil be kept within at the engine inlet of a MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7/S60ME-C10.7 two-stroke engine, and what happens if it drops too low?
gold_answer: Fuel viscosity at the engine inlet must stay between a minimum of 2 cSt and a maximum of 20 cSt, with normal operation around 3 cSt or higher for distillate fuel and 10-15 cSt for heavy fuel oil. If viscosity drops below the minimum, the fuel film becomes too thin to lubricate the fuel pump plungers and injection components properly, causing increased wear and risking fuel-pump/injector failure.
expected_points: minimum 2 cSt at engine inlet
maximum 20 cSt at engine inlet
normal distillate operation ~3 cSt or higher
normal HFO operation ~10-15 cSt
too-low viscosity causes inadequate lubrication and component wear
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Components for Fuel Oil System, p.285

question: What are the main quality limits for heavy fuel oil (HFO) accepted by these engines, and what happens if a bunker exceeds them?
gold_answer: Accepted HFO must have density at 15°C not exceeding 1.010 kg/m3, kinematic viscosity not exceeding 700 cSt at 50°C (55 cSt at 100°C), flash point at least 60°C, pour point not above 30°C, water content not more than 0.5% (v/v), and sulphur content not more than 4.5% (m/m). Fuel outside these limits tends to form combustion-chamber and gas-passage deposits and causes general combustion inefficiency, so it should be rejected or treated before use.
expected_points: density at 15°C <= 1.010 kg/m3
kinematic viscosity <= 700 cSt at 50°C
flash point >= 60°C, pour point <= 30°C
water <= 0.5% and sulphur <= 4.5%
out-of-spec fuel causes deposits and combustion inefficiency
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Fuel Oils, p.277 (S60ME-C10.7 p.265)

question: What fuel oil pressure must be maintained at the engine, and why does this matter?
gold_answer: Fuel oil pressure measured at the engine should be maintained at 7-8 bar, which corresponds to a circulating pump pressure of about 10 bar. Keeping the fuel pressurised this way prevents the fuel from gasifying (forming vapour bubbles) in the high-temperature fuel system, which would otherwise disrupt injection and degrade combustion.
expected_points: fuel pressure at engine ~7-8 bar
circulating pump pressure ~10 bar
insufficient pressure risks fuel gasification
gasification disrupts injection and combustion performance
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Fuel oil system, p.271 (S60ME-C10.7 p.257)

question: Why must heavy fuel oil piping be insulated and heat-traced, and what design limits apply?
gold_answer: Heavy fuel oil must stay hot enough to remain pumpable, so its piping is insulated (minimum 20 mm thickness) and heat-traced to maintain a pumping temperature of roughly 50°C. Insulation may only be fitted after the piping has passed and been approved in a pressure test, and the insulation's outer surface temperature must not exceed 55°C at a room temperature of up to 38°C. Without this, the fuel can cool and thicken to the point it can no longer be pumped, causing operational delays.
expected_points: minimum 20 mm insulation thickness
heat tracing maintains ~50°C pumping temperature
insulation fitted only after pressure test approval
max insulation surface temperature 55°C at 38°C room temperature
inadequate insulation risks inability to pump HFO
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Insulation and heat tracing, p.281 (S60ME-C10.7 p.269)

question: What system-oil specification is required for the crosshead/system lubricating oil, and what determines the size of its separator?
gold_answer: The system (crosshead) lubricating oil must meet an SAE 30 viscosity grade with a base number (BN) of 5-10. The oil separator serving this system is sized using a nominal capacity based on 0.136 litre per kW of total installed engine power, as recommended by the separator supplier.
expected_points: SAE 30 viscosity grade
base number (BN) 5-10
separator sized on 0.136 litre/kWh of installed power
unsuitable oil risks engine damage
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, System oil list/consumption, p.307 (S60ME-C10.7 p.295)

question: How is the minimum volume of the lubricating oil bottom tank determined, and what failure mode does an undersized tank risk?
gold_answer: The minimum bottom-tank volume equals the main lubricating-oil pump's rated (CEAS) capacity divided by 18, which limits the oil to at most 18 full circulations per hour. The tank must also have a symmetrical cross-section (to avoid bedplate distortion) and keep the pump suction always submerged. If the tank is undersized or suction is not kept submerged, the main LO pumps can draw in air, causing a supply failure that can seriously damage the main engine bearings.
expected_points: minimum tank volume = CEAS pump capacity / 18
limits circulation to max 18 times per hour
pump suction must stay submerged to avoid drawing in air
air ingestion risks LO supply failure and bearing damage
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Lubricating oil bottom tank, p.317 (S60ME-C10.7 p.305)

question: What inclination requirements apply to lubricating-oil system venting pipes, and why do they matter?
gold_answer: Venting pipes for the lubricating oil system must ascend steadily with a minimum longitudinal inclination of 5° and a minimum transverse inclination of 15°, with no pockets, and their sizes must comply with classification-society rules. Proper venting prevents condensate and foreign particles from accumulating in the system; if venting is inadequate, the lubricating oil can become contaminated, risking engine damage.
expected_points: minimum 5° longitudinal inclination
minimum 15° transverse inclination
no pipe pockets allowed, ascending routing
sizes must comply with classification-society rules
poor venting risks LO contamination and engine damage
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Venting and drain pipes, p.323 (S60ME-C10.7 p.311)

question: What cleanliness standard and flushing duration are required before commissioning a lubricating-oil system, and what are its running limits?
gold_answer: The lubricating-oil system must be flushed to reach an ISO 4406 XX/16/13 cleanliness level before commissioning, with flushing typically expected to take 15-26 hours. Once running, lubricating oil viscosity should be about 75 cSt at 50°C (up to 400 cSt tolerated for cold starts), maximum working temperature is 60°C, and the maximum differential pressure across the LO filter is 0.5 bar. Skipping proper flushing or exceeding these limits risks high differential pressure, filter clogging, and engine damage.
expected_points: ISO 4406 XX/16/13 cleanliness level required
flushing typically takes 15-26 hours
max working temperature 60°C
max differential pressure across LO filter 0.5 bar
poor flushing risks filter clogging and engine damage
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Components and installation, p.311 (S60ME-C10.7 p.299)

question: What are the key design parameters of the hydraulic control oil (HCO) system that supplies the engine's high-pressure pumps?
gold_answer: The hydraulic control oil (HCO) tank volume is sized at 10% of the hourly HCO pump flow rate, the maximum pump discharge pressure is 5 barg, and the oil must meet an ISO 4406 XX/16/13 cleanliness level. The return pipe must be sized so oil can flow back to the tank by natural gravity. Poor installation or maintenance of this system risks pressure buildup, leakage, and oil contamination that can cause system failure.
expected_points: tank volume = 10% of hourly HCO pump flow rate
max pump discharge pressure 5 barg
ISO 4406 XX/16/13 cleanliness required
return pipe sized for gravity flow
poor maintenance risks leakage/contamination/system failure
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Hydraulic control oil system, p.333 (S60ME-C10.7 p.321)

question: What viscosity range and minimum feed rate apply to cylinder oil on these engines, and why must the oil grade match the fuel?
gold_answer: Cylinder oil must have a kinematic viscosity of between 18.5 and 21.9 cSt at 100°C, and the minimum feed rate must not be less than 0.6 g/kWh. The specific cylinder oil grade (Category I or the higher-performance Category II) must be matched to the fuel's sulphur content, because an oil with the wrong alkalinity for the fuel in use leads to increased cylinder-liner/piston-ring wear.
expected_points: kinematic viscosity 18.5-21.9 cSt at 100°C
minimum feed rate 0.6 g/kWh
Category I vs Category II cylinder oils differ in performance
oil must be matched to fuel sulphur content to avoid increased wear
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Cylinder oil specification, p.341 (S60ME-C10.7 p.329)

question: What lubricating-oil pressure, temperature and viscosity limits apply to the turbocharger, and what failure can result if they're not met?
gold_answer: Turbocharger lubricating oil should have a viscosity of 75 cSt at 50°C, a maximum operating temperature of 70°C, and a maximum pump discharge pressure of 5 barg; the supply tank is sized at 10% of the pump flow rate. If the oil becomes contaminated or the level is not maintained, the turbocharger bearings can be starved or the pump can cavitate, leading to turbocharger failure.
expected_points: TC lube oil viscosity 75 cSt at 50°C
maximum TC lube oil temperature 70°C
maximum pump discharge pressure 5 barg
contamination or low oil level risks turbocharger bearing damage/failure
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Turbocharger lubricating oil, p.327 (S60ME-C10.7 p.315)

question: What pressure-loss limits apply across the exhaust gas boiler and the silencer/spark arrester, and what happens if they're exceeded?
gold_answer: The maximum recommended pressure loss across the exhaust gas boiler is normally 150 mm WC, and the combined pressure loss across the silencer and/or spark arrester should not exceed 100 mm WC at the specified MCR. Exceeding these limits increases back-pressure on the turbocharger/engine, reducing efficiency and risking operational problems.
expected_points: max pressure loss across exhaust gas boiler ~150 mm WC
combined silencer/spark-arrester loss <= 100 mm WC at MCR
excess back-pressure reduces engine/turbocharger efficiency
can lead to operational failures if ignored
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, System components (exhaust gas), p.457 (S60ME-C10.7 p.445)

question: What inhibitor regime is required for the low-temperature (LT) cooling water system, and how often must it be checked?
gold_answer: The LT cooling water system requires nitrite-borate-based corrosion inhibitors, maintained at the concentration specified by the manufacturer. Water samples should be tested weekly, and the system should be flushed and refilled annually. Neglecting inhibitor concentration leads to chemical corrosion that can damage cooling-system components.
expected_points: nitrite-borate based inhibitors required
weekly water sample testing
annual flush and refill
neglect causes chemical corrosion of cooling system components
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Low-temperature cooling water, p.373 (S60ME-C10.7 p.361)

question: What minimum inlet temperature must central (LT) cooling water be held at, and why does this matter?
gold_answer: Central (LT) cooling water inlet temperature must be kept at a minimum of 10°C, and the associated expansion tank volume must be at least 10% of the total central cooling water amount. Running the cooling water colder than this setpoint over-cools downstream consumers (lube oil, scavenge air), which increases fuel consumption and can lead to engine damage over time.
expected_points: minimum central cooling water inlet temperature 10°C
expansion tank volume >= 10% of system volume
too-cold cooling water increases fuel consumption
can cause engine damage if ignored
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Central cooling water system, p.377 (S60ME-C10.7 p.365)

question: What jacket (HT) cooling water temperature limits apply before and during engine loading, and what risks do they guard against?
gold_answer: Jacket cooling water must reach at least 50°C before the engine is loaded, and its outlet temperature must not exceed 80°C during operation, with a maximum water velocity of 3.0 m/s in the piping. Loading the engine on cold jacket water, or operating above the limit, risks cold corrosion (especially on high-sulphur fuel) and mechanical overload from uneven thermal expansion.
expected_points: minimum 50°C jacket water before loading the engine
maximum 80°C jacket water outlet temperature
maximum 3.0 m/s water velocity
violating limits risks cold corrosion and mechanical overload
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, High-temperature cooling water, p.397 (S60ME-C10.7 p.385)

question: What flow-rate and pressure limits apply to the jacket cooling water pump, and what happens if they are not met?
gold_answer: The jacket cooling water pump must deliver 100-110% of its stated capacity, with a pump head of 3.0 bar and a maximum pressure drop of 0.5 bar on the jacket water side; maximum working temperature is 100°C. Falling outside these limits risks inadequate cooling flow, engine overheating, and potential cooling-system or engine failure.
expected_points: pump flow 100-110% of stated capacity
pump head 3.0 bar
max pressure drop 0.5 bar on jacket water side
max working temperature 100°C
failure to meet limits risks overheating/engine damage
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Components (jacket water), p.411 (S60ME-C10.7 p.399)

question: What type and pressure requirements apply to the starting air compressors and receivers, and what happens if pressure isn't maintained?
gold_answer: Starting air compressors must be water-cooled, two-stage units with intercooling, delivering at 30 bar, and the starting-air receivers must be rated for the same 30 bar working pressure. Receiver capacity must provide air for 12 starts on a reversible engine or 6 starts on a non-reversible engine. If the required pressure or stored-air quantity is not maintained, the engine may be unable to start.
expected_points: compressors are water-cooled, two-stage with intercooling
delivery/working pressure 30 bar
capacity for 12 starts (reversible engine) or 6 starts (non-reversible)
insufficient pressure/air quantity prevents engine starting
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Components for starting air, p.425 (S60ME-C10.7 p.413)

question: Under what conditions do the auxiliary scavenge-air blowers start and stop automatically, and what happens if one of them fails?
gold_answer: The auxiliary blowers start automatically when the blower inlet pressure drops below a preset level, roughly corresponding to engine loads in the 25-40% range, and they continue running for about 30 minutes after engine shutdown to prevent overheating. If one blower fails, the other can continue operating without manual intervention, though scavenging may be degraded if both fail, risking poor engine performance or a failed start.
expected_points: auto-start below a preset inlet pressure near 25-40% load
run ~30 minutes after shutdown to prevent overheating
the remaining blower can operate alone if one fails
loss of both blowers risks inadequate scavenging and poor performance/starting failure
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Auxiliary blowers, p.435 (S60ME-C10.7 p.423)

question: What precaution applies when cleaning the scavenge air cooler, and what must be done with the resulting drain water?
gold_answer: Scavenge air cooler cleaning (with a grease-dissolving chemical media) must only be carried out while the engine is at standstill. If the oil content of the drain water exceeds 15 ppm, it must not be discharged overboard and must instead be routed to the oily bilge water holding tank.
expected_points: cleaning only performed with engine at standstill
drain water oil content limit of 15 ppm
water above that limit must go to the oily bilge holding tank, never overboard
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Scavenge air cooler cleaning, p.441

question: What fire-fighting media and quantities are specified for a scavenge-space fire, and what pressures must each system maintain?
gold_answer: A scavenge-space fire is fought with steam (about 3.2 kg per cylinder, supplied at 3-10 bar), water mist (about 2.6 kg per cylinder, with freshwater pressure of at least 3.5 bar), or CO2 (about 6.5 kg per cylinder, with the CO2 system tested at 150 bar). Failing to activate the correct system promptly risks catastrophic engine damage or fire spread.
expected_points: steam ~3.2 kg/cylinder at 3-10 bar
water mist ~2.6 kg/cylinder at >=3.5 bar freshwater
CO2 ~6.5 kg/cylinder, system tested at 150 bar
delayed activation risks catastrophic damage or fire spread
source_citation: MAN B&W S60ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Fire extinguishing system, p.435

question: How does the engine control system (ECS) achieve redundancy, and what happens if one control unit fails?
gold_answer: The ECS runs two engine control units (ECUs) in parallel plus a dedicated cylinder control unit (CCU) for every cylinder, and the whole system has two separate power supplies with battery backup. This redundancy means a single ECU or CCU failure typically causes only a partial loss of function, such as an engine slowdown, rather than a full engine shutdown.
expected_points: two ECUs operate in parallel
each cylinder has its own dedicated CCU
two separate power supplies with battery backup
single-unit failure causes slowdown/partial loss, not full shutdown
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Control system layout, p.479 (S60ME-C10.7 p.465)

question: When is a torsional vibration damper required on these engines, and what torsional frequency limits apply to the propeller shaft line?
gold_answer: A torsional vibration damper is required on 11- or 12-cylinder engines in the 98-80 bore range. Independently of that, the first-node torsional vibration frequency in the propeller shaft line should be kept above 3 Hz for fixed-pitch-propeller (FPP) plants and above 5 Hz for controllable-pitch-propeller (CPP) plants. Ignoring these requirements risks significant varying torque and annoying longitudinal vibration in the engine, double bottom or deckhouse.
expected_points: torsional vibration damper required for 11/12-cylinder, 98-80 bore-range engines
first-node torsional frequency > 3 Hz for FPP plants
first-node torsional frequency > 5 Hz for CPP plants
violating limits risks varying torque and structural/longitudinal vibration
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Axial and torsional vibration, p.509 (S60ME-C10.7 p.495)

question: What is Power Related Unbalance (PRU), and how are its risk bands for hull vibration interpreted?
gold_answer: Power Related Unbalance (PRU) expresses the engine's first- and second-order external moments relative to its power output, as an indicator of how likely those moments are to excite disturbing hull vibrations. A PRU of 0-60 is considered not relevant, 60-120 unlikely to cause problems, 120-220 likely to cause noticeable vibration, and above 220 most likely to cause disturbing hull vibrations, so higher cylinder-count/configuration choices with lower PRU are preferred where hull vibration is a concern.
expected_points: PRU compares 1st/2nd order external moments to engine power
0-60 PRU: not relevant
60-120: unlikely; 120-220: likely
above 220: most likely to cause disturbing hull vibration
source_citation: MAN B&W S60ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Power related unbalance, p.487

question: What design requirement applies to the engine's shutdown/slowdown sensors in an Unattended Machinery Space (UMS), and why?
gold_answer: In a UMS, the shutdown system must use independent sensors, or sensors wired with galvanically separated circuits, in line with IACS and classification-society requirements, and the shutdown/slowdown systems must be electrically separated from other systems. This prevents a single sensor or wiring failure from masking a genuine fault or from itself causing an unsafe engine condition, since there is no watchkeeping engineer present to intervene manually.
expected_points: independent sensors or galvanically separated circuits required
follows IACS/classification-society requirements
shutdown/slowdown systems kept electrically separate from other systems
prevents a single failure from causing unsafe unattended operation
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Slow down and shut down, p.523 (S60ME-C10.7 p.509)

question: What water-in-oil alarm thresholds protect the main bearings, and what long-term water-content limit must not be exceeded?
gold_answer: The water-in-oil monitoring system raises a high alarm at a water activity (aw) of 0.5 and a high-high alarm at 0.9. Independently of the alarm setpoints, water content in the lubricating oil should never exceed 0.2%, since higher sustained water content causes corrosive wear to the main/crosshead bearings.
expected_points: high alarm at water activity (aw) 0.5
high-high alarm at water activity (aw) 0.9
water content in LO must not exceed 0.2%
exceeding this causes corrosive bearing wear
source_citation: MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide, Engine protection systems, p.539 (S60ME-C10.7 p.525)

question: What is the function of a piston-rod stuffing box on a two-stroke crosshead engine, and why must its oil drain be monitored?
gold_answer: The piston-rod stuffing box seals the crankcase, which holds the clean system (crosshead) lubricating oil, from the scavenge space and cylinder below, preventing cylinder oil and combustion by-products from contaminating the system oil (and vice versa). The quantity of oil draining from the stuffing box is itself a monitored condition-based-maintenance indicator: a rising drain quantity suggests the sealing rings are wearing and need attention before a sealing failure allows cross-contamination.
expected_points: seals the crankcase (system oil) from the scavenge/cylinder space
prevents cross-contamination between system oil and cylinder oil/combustion products
stuffing-box drain quantity is a monitored CBM indicator
rising drain quantity indicates worn sealing rings
source_citation: general two-stroke crosshead-engine design knowledge (consistent with system-oil consumption discussion, MAN B&W S50ME-C10.7 Project Guide p.307)

question: What is condition-based maintenance (CBM), and how does it differ from the fixed-calendar survey regimes traditionally used by classification societies?
gold_answer: Condition-based maintenance triggers inspection or repair from the equipment's actually measured condition and trend (e.g. vibration levels, oil analysis results, bearing/alarm data) rather than from a fixed calendar interval. Classification societies now offer CBM-based survey schemes as a real alternative to fixed 5-year special surveys, provided the owner implements continuous monitoring and keeps the documented trend data the society requires to approve deferring or re-scoping a calendar-based survey.
expected_points: CBM triggers maintenance from measured condition/trend data, not a fixed calendar
example indicators: vibration, oil analysis, bearing/alarm data
classification societies offer CBM survey schemes as an alternative to fixed calendar surveys
requires documented continuous monitoring to qualify

question: Why is lubricating/system oil analysis a useful condition-monitoring tool for a marine engine?
gold_answer: Routine oil analysis (checking wear-metal particle content, water content, viscosity and total base number) can reveal developing problems such as bearing wear, cooling-water ingress, or fuel dilution well before they cause a failure. This supports predictive, condition-based maintenance instead of waiting for a fixed service interval or a reactive repair after something has already failed.
expected_points: wear-metal/particle analysis detects developing component wear
water content indicates cooling-water ingress/leaks
viscosity/TBN trend shows oil degradation
supports predictive/condition-based maintenance over reactive repair
source_citation: general domain knowledge, consistent with NAVEDTRA Joint Oil Analysis Program Manual (afd-070730-009)

question: How does MARPOL Annex VI constrain a Chief Engineer's choices when operating the main engine, with respect to NOx and fuel sulphur?
gold_answer: MARPOL Annex VI sets NOx emission Tier limits that are tied to the engine's EIAPP (Engine International Air Pollution Prevention) certificate and its approved parameter record, so the engineer cannot freely alter injection timing or other approved settings without class/flag approval. It also sets fuel sulphur content limits, both globally and more strictly inside Emission Control Areas (ECAs/SECAs), which requires the engine to follow a documented fuel changeover procedure (e.g. to a low-sulphur distillate) before entering an ECA.
expected_points: NOx Tier limits tied to the engine's EIAPP certificate and approved parameters
engineer cannot deviate from approved settings without class/flag approval
global and stricter ECA/SECA fuel sulphur limits apply
requires a documented fuel changeover procedure before entering an ECA
